## 3BS · ✅ THE AMT WARNING IS ONLY THE AUDI — and on the evidence it is CORRECT, not an error

> **Lilian, 2026-09-28:** *"¿Por qué está saliendo esto solo por el Audi? Revisé los otros assets y no veo
> que haya diferencia entre la depreciación AMT y el impuesto regular… El Audi lo incluyó Julia. En años
> anteriores, yo simplemente lo dejé como estaba. ¿Hay alguna forma de arreglarlo?"*

### ① 🔑 WHAT THE WARNING IS ACTUALLY TESTING

**One thing: does this asset's AMT depreciation column differ from its federal column?** ✅ **She checked
every asset and only the Audi does. That observation is the useful fact, and the rest follows from it.**

### ② ✅ WHY IT IS THE AUDI AND NOTHING ELSE — three facts the return itself supplies

**Property gets an AMT depreciation adjustment when it is depreciated 200DB for regular tax, because AMT
uses 150DB over the same life.** 🔑 **TWO THINGS SWITCH THAT ADJUSTMENT OFF, and between them they cover
every asset on this schedule except one:**

| Asset | Why it has NO Fed/AMT difference |
|---|---|
| `#1800` · `#7107` · `2019 Wabash` · `2023 Utility Trailer` | ✅ **They TOOK BONUS** *(their `Special allowance` column is the full cost)*. **Property that takes bonus gets no AMT depreciation adjustment at all** |
| `2022 Frght Cascadia` · `2025 Benson` | ✅ **They took NO bonus — but they were placed in service in 2024, and the 2024 return filed an ELECTION OUT for 3-year and 5-year property** *(§3A-bis ④)*. 📄 **Form 4562 (2025) instructions: property electing out *"will not be subject to an AMT adjustment for depreciation"*** |
| `FRT'18(HU4577)` | 🟡 **Took no bonus either, and shows no difference — so 2020 presumably elected out too.** ⚠️ **NOT ESTABLISHED: the firm does not hold the 2020 return** |
| 🔴 **`AUDI`** | 🛑 **It took NO bonus AND it has no election behind it** — ③ |

### ③ 🔑 AND THE PROOF THAT 2021 CANNOT HAVE ELECTED OUT — it is on this return's own schedule

🛑 **The §168(k) election out is made BY CLASS and covers ALL property in that class placed in service
that year** *(§3BI ②, quoted from the instructions)*.

⇒ **`#1800` (7/20/2021) and `#7107` (6/16/2021) are FIVE-YEAR assets placed in service in 2021, and they
BOTH took bonus — 30,245 and 28,145.** ⇒ 🔑 **So there was no election out of 5-year property in 2021.**
**The Audi is a 5-year asset placed in service 2/1/2021.** ⇒ ⛔ **Its zero bonus is therefore NOT AN
ELECTION.** ⚠️ 🆕 **NARROWED IN REVIEW: whether the §280F cap absorbed the bonus or the preparer simply did
not claim it is NOT established — §3AW gives the Audi a recovery basis of the full 50,020 and a 2025
charge of 2,881, which is the UNCAPPED year-five rate, so no cap is visibly operating in the software.**
✅ **The conclusion does not turn on which: neither route is a class election, so either way the AMT
adjustment applies.**

✅ **WHICH MEANS THE AUDI IS THE ONE ASSET ON THIS SCHEDULE THAT IS GENUINELY SUBJECT TO THE AMT
DEPRECIATION ADJUSTMENT.** 🔑 **The difference she is seeing is the law working, not a keying mistake.**

### ④ ✅ AND THE RETURN CORROBORATES IT IN TWO PLACES

| | |
|---|---|
| **K-1 box 15B `Adjusted gain or loss` = −3,719** | 🔑 **This line exists ONLY when a DISPOSED asset had a different AMT basis from its regular basis.** ⚠️ 🆕 **CORRECTED IN REVIEW: box 17K carries TWO assets, not three — `#1800` 4,500 + `#7107` 20,000 = 24,500 *(§3BL ②)* — and `FRT'18(HU4577)` is a SECOND non-§179 2025 disposal, reported on Form 4797 Part III** *(§3C)*. ⇒ ⛔ **So the Audi is NOT the only non-§179 disposal, and box 15B does not point at it by elimination.** ✅ **What DOES point at it is ①'s observation — Lilian checked every asset and only the Audi shows a Fed/AMT difference, so only the Audi can be contributing to 15B** |
| **K-1 box 15A `Post-1986 depreciation adjustment` = −1,809, NEGATIVE** | ✅ **Consistent too. By year five, 150DB gives MORE annual depreciation than 200DB** *(200DB front-loads)*, **so AMT exceeds regular and the adjustment goes negative.** ⓘ **§3AW already attributes the −1,809 to the AUDI** |

### ⑤ ☑️ SO: IS THERE A WAY TO FIX IT? — and the recommendation is **LEAVE IT**

⛔ **There is nothing to fix, on this reading.** ✅ **RECOMMENDATION: leave the Audi exactly as it is.**
**Four reasons, in order:**

1. 🔑 **It is probably correct.** ③ and ④ both point the same way.
2. 💵 **The amount is small and it does not touch this return at all.** **The corporation pays no AMT

   was disposed of on 8/21/2025, so whatever is keyed is the last thing this asset ever does.**
4. ✅ **It is Julia's asset and Lilian's standing rule already covers it** *(decision 94)*.

## 3BT · 🔑 WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING IN THE EQUITY SECTION — and yes, there is a problem, but not the one it looks like

> **Lilian, 2026-09-28:** *"Explícame qué es lo que está pasando con el paid-in capital y el additional
> paid-in capital. ¿Hay algún problema con eso? No entiendo qué está sucediendo."*

### ① 🔑 THE SITUATION IN ONE PARAGRAPH, before any line numbers

**Over the years this company has PAID OUT to its owner far more than it has ever earned, and far more
than he ever put in.** ⇒ **That drives the equity section of the balance sheet deeply negative.**
**Somebody has to decide which equity LINE absorbs it, and the 2024 return put it in
`Additional paid-in capital` — which is why that line prints as a NEGATIVE number.**
🔑 **That is the whole of it. It is not a mistake in the books; it is a consequence of how the money moved.**

### ② 📋 THE THREE LINES, AND WHAT EACH IS SUPPOSED TO HOLD

| Schedule L | Name | What it means | On this return |
|---|---|---|---|
| **22** | **`Capital stock`** | **What he paid for his shares at the very beginning** | **1,000** |
| **23** | **`Additional paid-in capital`** | 🔑 **Everything ELSE he has contributed — money he put in without buying more shares and without lending it** | 🔴 **(61,169) — NEGATIVE** |
| **24** | **`Retained earnings`** | **Profit the company made and has not paid out.** Negative = an accumulated deficit | ⚠️ 🆕 **7,349** *(§3BY ①; it read 3,349 before the 4,000)* |

⇒ 🛑 **AND THAT IS WHY A NEGATIVE LINE 23 IS ODD TO PRINT: a figure whose job is to measure *what the
owner PUT IN* cannot really be less than zero.** **He did not contribute minus 61,169.**
✅ **What it actually represents is distributions the AAA could not absorb, parked there.**

### ③ ✅ WHERE (61,169) CAME FROM — three printed figures on the 2024 return and one exact identity

| 2024 return | |
|---|---|
| Schedule K line 16d — total distributions | **113,157** |
| Schedule M-2 line 7 — what ran through the AAA | **51,988** |
| Schedule M-2 line 8 — closing AAA | **ZERO** |
| Schedule L line 23 | **(61,169)** |

✅ **113,157 − 51,988 = 61,169, to the dollar.** 🔑 **The accumulated adjustments account absorbed
everything it had and went to zero; the remainder is what line 23 carries.**
⚠️ **Stated as three printed figures and an identity — NOT as what the preparer decided, because nobody
has asked her** *(§3AE ②; decision 51 is Lilian deferring exactly that)*.

### ④ 🔴 SO IS THERE A PROBLEM? — FOUR answers, and only one of them is about this return

| | The question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Is it a problem for the COMPANY's tax?** | ⛔ **No.** **An 1120-S does not tax equity. Not one figure on page 1 moves** |
| **2** | 🔴 **Is it a problem for the OWNER?** | 🛑 **POSSIBLY, AND THIS IS THE REAL ONE.** **Distributions in excess of his STOCK BASIS are taxable to him as capital gain** *(§1368(b)(2))*. **An equity section this deeply negative is exactly what a basis problem looks like from the outside** — ⛔ **and the firm does not hold his Form 7203** *(§8B)*. **It is HIS return, not this one, but it is the same money** |
| **3** | **Is it a presentation problem?** | 🟡 **Yes, mildly.** **A negative paid-in capital is the line a bank or a reviewer stops on, because it says he took out far more than he ever contributed. A negative RETAINED EARNINGS would say the same thing and is completely ordinary to read** *(§3BM ①ⓑ — both options, and neither changes any tax)* |
| **4** | 🔑 **Is some of it not a distribution at all?** | ✅ 🆕 **ANSWERED 2026-09-28 — NO. LILIAN RULED: what is not a liability, a business expense or something the firm can compute IS distributions, and there is no shareholder loan in either direction** *(decision 104, §3BW)*. **Schedule L lines 7 and 19 stay blank because that is correct.** _(As written:)_ 🛑 THAT IS THE QUESTION WORTH ASKING, and it is question 1 of the client message — if part of what he took is a LOAN it belongs on line 7 as an ASSET |

### ⑤ 💵 AND WHAT 2025 ADDS TO IT

**The balance sheet needs closing equity of −162,063** *(§3BP ②)*. **With 1,000 of capital stock, the
(61,169) carried forward and 7,349 of book profit, it is short by 109,243 — and that 109,243 is 2025's
own version of the same movement.** ⚠️ 🆕 *(it read 3,349 and 105,243 before the 2015 trailer sale was
keyed on 2026-09-28 evening — §3BY ②)*

| | Line 23 | Line 24 |
|---|---|---|
| ⚖️ **Option A — charge 2025's to retained earnings** | **(61,169)** *(frozen at 2024's)* | 🔑 **(101,894)** ✅ *(unmoved by the 4,000)* |
| ⚖️ **Option B — the 2024 pattern, continued** | 🔑 **(170,412)** *(= 61,169 + 109,243)* | **7,349** |

✅ **Both total −162,063. Neither changes one number of tax.** ✅ 🆕 **CORRECTED 2026-09-28 — IT IS
JULIA'S PRESENTATION CALL TO CONFIRM OR OVERTURN, AND IT DOES NOT BLOCK: key OPTION B now and Schedule L
balances** *(decision 104, §3BW ⑤)*. _(As written:)_ 🛑 It is JULIA's presentation call, and it is the only

instalments, and the unpaid balance sits on Schedule L as a liability.** ⛔ 🆕 **LINE 17, not 20 — decision 136** *(§3CE ⑤ⓕ)*.

### ① 🔍 WHAT WENT WRONG, NAMED — because a diagnosis that is not specific cannot be followed

**The two explanations she names are §3BY ⑤ and ⑥. Read back, they do all of this:**

| What the writing did | Why it broke |

| 🔴 **Invented an abstraction she never asked for** — *"Model A / Model B"* | **She has to learn a vocabulary before she can learn the fact.** **There is no Model A. There is a company that bought insurance in September** |

### ② 🚚 MITSUBISHI — told in order

The client bought a trailer — the `2022 Benson` — on credit from Mitsubishi. During 2025 he paid them
instalments. Of everything he paid them that year, **1,823.59** was interest and **2,894.11** was principal.

We know both figures exactly, because the firm holds Mitsubishi's own document. So she is right: the loan is
closed, and nothing about the debt is open.

What is still open has nothing to do with Mitsubishi. It is about the client's own spreadsheet.

He sent an income statement with one line reading `equipment payments 102,834`. The firm checked what is
inside that line and found the full-year payments of six lenders. Mitsubishi is not one of them. So there are
exactly two possibilities, and they lead to opposite entries.

**Possibility 1 — he left Mitsubishi out by mistake.** This is the likely one. His payments are outside the
102,834 and are nowhere else in his P&L either. Then the firm **adds the 1,823.59 of interest to line 13**,
because it is a real expense he did not report. Without it we deduct too little.

**Possibility 2 — he put them inside a different line.** Specifically inside `Auto Repairs & Maintenance`,
which is 54,032. Then if the firm also adds the interest and the principal from the documents, the same money
is deducted twice, and **4,717.70 — everything he paid Mitsubishi in 2025, interest and principal together —
has to come out of line 20**. There we deduct too much.

And that is all the 6,541.29 ever was: `1,823.59 + 4,717.70`. It is the distance between the two
possibilities. It is not a fee, not a benefit, not a figure on any document, and nobody is claiming it.

### ③ 🛡️ IPFS AND THE INSURANCE — told in order

In September 2025 the client took out the insurance on the trucks. The premium for the whole year is
**35,593**. He did not pay it in one go. It worked like this:

1. A company called IPFS paid the insurer the whole premium, at once, in September.
2. From October the client repays IPFS **3,138.90** a month.
3. In 2025 he only got as far as October, November and December, plus a 10.00 set-up charge — **9,426.70**
   left his bank in total.
4. At 31 December he still owes IPFS the rest. That balance is a liability on the balance sheet.

Up to here she and the firm agree, and her description of it was right.

The open question is one sentence: on the 2025 return, how much goes on the insurance line?

- **Answer A — 35,593.** The insurer was paid in full in September. When someone lends you money and the
  expense gets paid with it, the expense counts as paid, even though you still owe the lender.
- ⛔ **Answer B — SUPERSEDED.** ⚠️ **And it was never 9,426.70 even on its own terms: a cash model is `15,753.60`, because the 6,336.90 down payment is cash paid for insurance too** *(decision 136)*. ✅ **DECISION 135 TAKES THE PREMIUM.** _(As written: **Answer B — 9,426.70.** Only what actually left the client's bank in 2025.)_

The difference is ⛔ 🆕 **`20,872.61` — decision 136; this line read **26,166**, which double-counted the down payment** — **and it is the largest open deduction left on this return. The firm does not**
decide it and has keyed nothing. It is **Julia's** — she signs.

And one thing could make all of it irrelevant: nobody knows what is inside his `Insurance` line of 79,963.
If he already put the whole premium in there, the deduction is taken and nothing moves. ⛔ 🆕 **HE DID, AND THAT LAST CLAUSE IS WRONG — 2026-09-30, §3CC ⑦ⓑ: the deduction is taken and the Schedule L liability is still missing, so something DOES move.** If he only put in
what he paid, the difference is live. ✅ 🆕 **ANSWERED 2026-09-30 — decision 135: the PREMIUM is the deduction and the loan balance is a Schedule L LINE 17 liability** *(§3CE ⑤)*. _(As written: "the 26,166 is live. That is exactly what client question 4 now asks.")_

One thing is already settled: that 79,963 is nowhere near all IPFS. The policy IPFS financed covers damage to

−10,294 back to −14,294.**

the §1245/§1250 class for the Part III computation, which Part II bypasses)*. ✅ **Leave cost and depreciation
blank. Leave `Holding period` as it falls.**

wrong, and a reviewer would catch it.**

line 24 or 25a"*, and line 25a is *"Depreciation allowed or allowable from line 22"*.** **ATX is not
shortcutting anything.**

🔑 **And Part III is NOT wrong in principle — it is UNFILLABLE HERE.** **Form 4797 line 22 asks for**
*"Deductions allowed or allowable for depreciation"* ⚠️ 🆕 *(that is the INSTRUCTIONS' Line 22 Step 1; the FORM's own line 22 reads "Depreciation (or depletion) allowed or allowable" — attribution corrected in review)*. **Filled properly for a fully depreciated trailer — line 21
= its cost, line 22 = the same cost — Part III gives line 23 = 0, line 24 = 4,000, line 25a = the cost, and
line 25b = 4,000 for any cost of 4,000 or more.** ✅ **The SAME destination as line 10.** ⛔ **So Part III is
not the wrong section. It is a section we cannot fill, because nobody knows what the trailer cost.**

✅ **AND THIS RETURN ALREADY CONTAINS THE PROOF, in its own Part III column A.** **The `FRT'18` is the
trailer's structural twin — fully depreciated, sold at a gain: cost 46,000, depreciation 46,000, adjusted basis
0, total gain 6,000.** **Its whole 6,000 became ORDINARY through line 25b — and it did so ONLY because line 22
carried 46,000.** 🔑 **The trailer's line 22 is empty, and there is no document to fill it.**

⇒ ✅ **THE SENTENCE FOR JULIA:** **Part II line 10 computes its gain as *(d) + (e) − (f)*, so with proceeds of
4,000 and any cost C entered as both the depreciation and the basis it returns 4,000 — and with both blank it
returns 4,000 as well.** **It reaches the answer WITHOUT asserting a cost the firm cannot establish, and the
firm's standing rule is never to invent a figure to fill a box.**

### ⑧ ⚠️ THREE HONEST CAVEATS ON THAT POSITION — recorded so a reviewer sees they were considered

**a) The de minimis banner is a SUPPORTING citation, not the authority.** 🔑 **The rule ATX prints IS the IRS
instruction — Form 4797 (2025), Line 10: *"If you receive ordinary income from a sale or other disposition of
property and deducted the cost of the property under the tangible property de minimis safe harbor, report the
income on line 10."*** ⛔ **But every version of it is CONDITIONAL on that deduction actually having been taken
under that safe harbor, which needs accounting procedures in place at the start of the year — WRITTEN ones only where the taxpayer has an applicable financial statement — and an annual election — and §3AV ②'s three
histories do not include it.** ✅ **The better ground is decision 67's own: §1245 recapture runs on depreciation
*allowed OR allowable*.**

**b) The residual exposure runs AGAINST the taxpayer, which is why it is not a reason to change.** 🔑 **If the
trailer cost less than 4,000 and no de minimis election was ever made, part of the 4,000 was §1231 gain rather
than ordinary income, and this return over-reports ORDINARY income.** ⛔ **The paper earlier put a ceiling of
≈1,500 on that; the ceiling does not hold — it could reach the whole 4,000.** ✅ **In every version it means
MORE tax to the shareholder, not less. Nobody is assessed for that.**

**c) TWO QUESTIONS THE REPOSITORY CANNOT ANSWER, and both are JULIA'S:**

1. ⚖️ **Whether the COMPANY or the SHAREHOLDER owned the trailer** *(decision 67 already flags it — if the
   shareholder owned it, the sale is not the company's and the 4,000 is a CONTRIBUTION)*.
2. ⚖️ 🆕 **If the company §179'd it back in 2015, it may not be a corporate Form 4797 item at all.**
   **Decision 87 holds that a §179 asset's disposal goes to Schedule K line 17d and K-1 BOX 17 CODE K, and that
   page 1 line 4 does NOT move.** ⚠️ **§3AV ② lists *"expensed the purchase (or §179'd it)"* as one of its
   three histories and treats all three as giving the same answer — they give the same CHARACTER, ordinary, but
   not the same LINE.** ✅ **The 4,000 reaches the shareholder as ordinary either way; where it is reported
   differs.**

⚠️ **AND ONE CAVEAT FROM §3F THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH ANY ANSWER ON THIS ASSET:** **the zero-basis premise is
stamped there as *a READING, not a fact* — under one unresolved reading the asset IS on the schedule under
another name and DOES carry basis.** **It was keyed anyway, on decision 67's balance of histories.**

car and hands it back. It never owns it.**

nothing on Schedule L — no asset line and no liability line.** ✅ **The payments are simply a deduction.**

expense.** ⛔ **Not line 13** — a lease payment is not interest. ⛔ **Not line 14** — there is nothing to
depreciate.

**How much for 2025: 2,383.24.** **That is `595.81 × 4`, September through December.** 🔑 **August is zero
because the 12,578.97 due at signing — which included the first monthly payment — was settled entirely by
rebates and non-cash credits. The company paid no cash in August, and this return is on the cash basis.**

### ② ⚠️ AND THE ANSWER TO *"¿TENEMOS ALGO REPORTADO HASTA AHORA?"* IS: NOTHING HAS BEEN ADDED

|---|---|

settles all three.**

`PURCHASER'S SIGNATURE`, `SALES REPRESENTATIVE` and all four `DATE` lines are blank, and therefore that the
firm holds NO acquisition document for ANY 2025 truck.**

⛔ **THE CAUSE IS NOT CARELESSNESS AND IT WAS NOT A PERSON'S ERROR.** **Every one of those values lives in
the PDF's FILLABLE FORM FIELDS, and the firm's own redactor did not read form fields at all until
[PR #485](https://github.com/JuliaJKAcct/JKAccountingGroup/pull/485) landed on `main` — 2026-09-29, the day

### ② ⚖️ SO WHAT DECISION 75 SHOULD HAVE SAID — and it changes the ask, not the figures

✅ **The `1840` invoice is a dealer's invoice ADDRESSED TO ZAKOM INCORPORATED, DATED 06/25/2025, carrying an
invoice number and a customer number, for stock `263894`, at 115,000.00 plus a 550.00 dealer prep charge =
115,550.00.**
⚠️ **It is still UNSIGNED by the purchaser and by the dealership manager, and the form's own terms say it is
not binding until a dealership representative signs.**

🔑 **WHAT THAT IS WORTH, PRECISELY:** **it establishes the SELLER, the BUYER, the VEHICLE, the PRICE and the
DATE, from the seller's own system.** ⛔ **It does not prove the money moved.** ✅ **For a depreciation
schedule that is enough and more than the firm has for three of the other five additions** — **and the
cost it states already matches the booked figure to the dollar.**

⚠️ **AND ONE THING THE INVOICE DOES *NOT* ESTABLISH, which an earlier draft of this subsection treated as
settled:** **the `1840`'s census date reads `Jul 2025` and the invoice's `Contract Date` is `06/25/2025`** —
🔑 **but a CONTRACT date is not a PLACED-IN-SERVICE date.** ⛔ **The paper keeps those distinct on purpose:
§3BE ④ reads ACQUISITION dates off contracts and says so, while the in-service column is the client's.**
**An unsigned invoice dated 25 June is evidence the deal was struck in June; the truck could still have been
delivered in July.**
✅ **AND NO FIGURE TURNS ON IT EITHER WAY: under the HALF-YEAR convention an asset takes half a year whatever
the month** *(decision 54)*, **and Q2 versus Q3 does not move the mid-quarter test — Q4's share is unchanged
at 23,000 of 421,485, 5.46%, nowhere near 40%.** ☑️ **So record the invoice date as what it is — the CONTRACT
date, documented — and move the in-service field only if the client or a delivery document says June.**

### ① ⚖️ THE GAIN IS STILL A 2025 ITEM — and the reasoning is not the one the paper used

🛑 **§3AY resolved *"does the casualty belong on this return at all"* by finding the 57,500 credit on
9 April 2025** *(decision 73)*. ✅ **That conclusion survives. The ARGUMENT under it has changed and should be
restated, because the old one no longer fits the facts.**

**The old reasoning ran: the truck was destroyed in 2025 and the money arrived in 2025, so the whole event is
2025.** ⛔ **Half of that is now false.**

✅ **THE REASONING THAT ACTUALLY HOLDS:**

1. 🔑 **A casualty produces a realized GAIN when the property is converted INTO MONEY**, not when it is
   destroyed. ✅ **AND THIS IS NOT A NEW RULE — IT IS THE FIRM'S OWN, WRITTEN MONTHS AGO.** **Decision 13a ③,
   quoted at §3AI ⑥:** *"gain is realized when the PROCEEDS ARE RECEIVED, which may fall in a different tax
   year from the loss."* **It is restated on four more live surfaces — §3AP ①, §3AR ② row 3, §3BX ⑥ and the
   §6 checklist — each in the form *"what matters is when the INSURER PAID, not when the truck was
   destroyed."*** 🛑 **The paper had the rule five times over and nobody had the fact to apply it to: every
   surface assumed the loss was in 2025.** **On 31 December 2024 this company had a destroyed truck and an
   unsettled claim: an amount nobody could yet fix.**
2. **This return is prepared on the CASH basis, and it is stated on the return itself rather than inferred:**
   **Schedule B line 1 reads `Cash` on the FILED 2024 return** *(§1's comparative — `Accounting method
   (Sch B line 1) | CASH`)*, **and the keyed 2025 draft reproduces it** *(§3AW — `Accounting method | Cash
   (box a)`)*. ⇒ **The 57,500 is income WHEN RECEIVED: 9 April 2025.** ✅ **There is no accrual question and
   no 12/31/2024 receivable to argue about, which is what makes the 2024 loss date harmless to the year.**
3. ⇒ **The gain is realized in 2025 and is reported on the 2025 return.**

⚠️ **AND THE BRANCH THAT DIED STAYS DEAD.** **§3AU ②'s table carried *"nothing in 2025 ⇒ the casualty is a
2026 item and comes off this return"*.** ⛔ **A 2024 loss date does not resurrect it** — **the money arrived in
2025, and the year of the MONEY is the year of the gain.**

🔑 **WHAT WOULD HAVE MADE THIS A 2024 RETURN ITEM, and did not happen: a casualty LOSS.** **A loss belongs to
the year of the loss.** ⛔ **There is no loss here — the adjusted basis is ZERO, so the event can only ever
produce a gain.** ✅ **Which means 2024 needed nothing, and needs nothing now.**

### ② ✅ THE §1033 CLOCK DOES NOT MOVE — it runs from the gain, not from the wreck

**§3AY ③ and decision 13a put the replacement period at 12/31/2027 for a 2025 realization.**
🔑 **§1033(a)(2)(B) measures the period from the close of the FIRST TAXABLE YEAR IN WHICH ANY PART OF THE GAIN
IS REALIZED.** **The gain is realized in 2025** *(① above)* ⇒ **the period still ends 12/31/2027.**
⛔ **It does NOT run from 17 December 2024.**
⚠️ **§1033 is cited from knowledge here as it is everywhere else in this paper** — ✅ **and nothing turns on
it, because decision 83 already raised the deferral and recommended AGAINST it, and nobody has asked for it.**

⚠️ **DECISION 86 KEYED `04/09/2025` AND CALLED IT PROVISIONAL, IN LILIAN'S OWN WORDS, PENDING THE CLIENT.**
🗣️ **Her reasoning was:** *"puse la fecha en la que el camión fue siniestrado como la misma fecha en la que se
recibió el dinero… es poco probable que ese mismo día haya sido siniestrado"*, **and she judged that a loss
two months before the money was at least as plausible as one three months before it.**
✅ **She was right that the date on his sheet was a placeholder. The answer simply sat OUTSIDE the range
anyone was considering — the loss was nearly FOUR months before the money, and in the PRIOR TAX YEAR.**

|---|---|

The conversion into money completed on 9 April 2025, and that is the event this return reports.** ⇒ **A 2025 return showing a 2025 disposition is internally consistent, and it is what ATX's §179 disposition report is built for** |

anything written for the reviewer.** ⚠️ **If Julia prefers the loss date in the field, it costs nothing to

### ④ 🔧 THE 23,500 SURVIVES — and on a BETTER footing than it had this morning

**§3CC ⑧ⓑ computed the casualty at 23,500: 57,500 received, less the ≈34,000 of towing it reimbursed,
against a ZERO adjusted basis.** ✅ **The figure does not move.** ⚠️ **But one of the two arguments under it
has to be replaced, and the replacement is stronger.**

🔑 **THE ARGUMENT THAT NO LONGER WORKS.** **§3CC ⑧ⓑ reasoned that if the towing WERE inside his P&L, you would
add 34,000 of income and keep the 34,000 deduction and still reach 23,500 — a SAME-YEAR netting argument.**
⛔ **If the truck was destroyed on 17 December 2024, the tow was very probably paid in DECEMBER 2024**, **and
a 2024 expense cannot be netted against 2025 income inside one year.**

✅ **THE ARGUMENT THAT REPLACES IT IS SIMPLER AND IS A STATUTE.** **He never deducted the towing — his own
words, decision 117.** ⇒ **The 34,000 he received back is the recovery of a cost that produced NO tax
benefit, so there is nothing to bring into income** *(the tax-benefit principle of §111, and more directly:
an unclaimed cost reimbursed is a return of outlay, not profit)*. ⇒ **Only the excess over that cost is a
gain, and the truck's basis is zero.**

```
  insurance received, 9 April 2025                57,500
  less the towing it reimbursed, never deducted (34,000)
  ------------------------------------------------------
  attributable to the VEHICLE                     23,500
  less the vehicle's adjusted basis                    0
  ------------------------------------------------------
  SECTION 1245 ORDINARY INCOME, 2025              23,500
```

🔑 **AND THE YEAR OF THE TOW NO LONGER MATTERS TO THE ANSWER** — **which is exactly why this footing is
better.** ⛔ **Under the old netting argument it would have mattered a great deal.**

🔴 **ONE NEW OPEN ITEM, AND IT IS NOT SMALL — THE 12/17/2024 LOSS DATE MOVED THE TOWING'S DEDUCTION YEAR TO
THE ONE YEAR NOTHING HERE HAS CHECKED.** ⛔ **AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH CALLED IT *"a confirmation
and not a search"* ON THREE READINGS. IT IS WITHDRAWN: none of the three reaches 2024's DEDUCTION.**

🔑 **THE WHOLE 23,500 RESTS ON ONE FACT — that the 34,000 of towing is a cost the company BORE and NEVER
DEDUCTED.** **If it was paid AND deducted in 2024, the 2025 recovery is income under §111 — 34,000 of
CORPORATE other income with no offsetting deduction, not box 17K. That is larger than any figure this batch

is recorded here rather than silently corrected, because CLAUDE.md's ask-don't-guess rule makes a
mis-transcription a QUESTION TO PUT, never one to reason around, and page 1 line 1a is the largest single
figure typed on this return.** ⚠️ **A session reading only the quote would key a hundred thousand less.**

✅ **DECIDED. Page 1 line 1a stays at the client's `1,289,315` and nothing is added to it.**
⛔ **The question §3CC ⑦ⓒ raised — whether his revenue is the GROSS freight billed or the money that reached
his account after his partner withheld ≈44,370 of insurance premiums — is NOT acted on.**
⇒ **Decision 119 closes, the new client question comes off the list, and the free bank sweep of freight
credits is no longer required.**

🔑 **AND IT IS THE STANDING RULE, NOT AN EXCEPTION.** **Decision 7 — Julia's, 2026-09-13:** *"We have to rely
on the P&L numbers from the client. We're not going to be doing any verifications from it."* **Decision 105
sharpened it a fortnight later: the firm reconstructs what a DOCUMENT states and does not complete a caption
the client under-reported.** ✅ **This is that rule applied to the income side.**

🛑 **AND THE OBJECTION IS RECORDED RATHER THAN ERASED, BECAUSE IT TRAVELS TO THE SIGNER.**
**[`tax-return-sop`](../../../.claude/skills/tax-return-sop/) §4C:** *where the paper records an objection
that was overruled, the objection travels to the reviewer WITH the decision — she is the one who signs.*
**So, stated once, plainly, for Julia's briefing and not as a re-argument:**

| | |
|---|---|
| **What the client said** | **His freight partner deducted the liability and cargo premiums from the freight it paid him, weekly** |
| **What his books do** | **They carry the full ≈44,370 as an insurance expense** |
| **What nobody established** | **Whether his `Sales Revenue` of 1,289,315 is the freight he BILLED or the cash that REACHED him** |
| 🔴 **The exposure if it is the cash** | **Gross receipts and net income are each understated by ≈44,370** — ⚠️ **and it runs AGAINST the client** |
| ⚖️ **The position taken** | **The client's figure is used, under decisions 7 and 105.** **The firm did not verify it, as it does not verify any of his captions** |
| ✅ **Why the position is defensible** | **It is the same treatment every other caption on this return gets, applied consistently** — ⛔ **and the alternative is to adjust a client's stated revenue on an inference nobody has tested** |

🔑 **THAT IS THE WHOLE OF IT: a decision somebody made, written down, rather than a thing nobody noticed.**
**The precedent is decision 1A's reading of Gossip Miami — *"an undocumented position is the one that loses"*.**
⛔ **It is not raised again with Lilian, and it is not an action item for Julia. It is a briefing line.**

### ⑧ 🎯 THE NEAR-MISS, AND THE FALSE DICHOTOMY — two things worth keeping about HOW this was got wrong

#### ⓐ ✅ A QUALIFIER ADDED ON REVIEW IS WHAT SAVES THIS RETURN, AND IT HAS NOW BEEN TESTED

🔑 **§3AI ⑥ carries three qualifiers that a reviewer added to the rule *"a casualty turns on when the insurer
paid"*. The FIRST of them is the one that matters here:**

> ⛔ ***"It holds for a GAIN, not for a LOSS. A casualty LOSS belongs to the year of the loss, so a 2025 loss…"***

⚠️ **THAT QUALIFIER WAS BRANCH-DEPENDENT WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN, AND THE BRANCH HAS NOW BEEN TESTED.**
🛑 **Had `#7107` carried any adjusted basis — had the 2021 return not consumed the whole 78,145 in §179 and
bonus — this would have been a casualty LOSS, and a 17 December 2024 loss date would have taken it OFF THIS
RETURN ENTIRELY and onto 2024's.**
✅ **It is a gain only because the basis is zero.** 🔑 **The qualifier was written against a hypothetical and
the hypothetical arrived.** ☑️ **Worth knowing the next time somebody is tempted to trim a qualifier that
looks redundant.**

⚠️ **AND THE COUNTERFACTUAL ITSELF IS NARROWER THAN IT FIRST READS — corrected in review, because this is
written down as a rule to REUSE.** 🔑 **A casualty LOSS covered by a claim that is still outstanding, with a
reasonable prospect of recovery, is NOT sustained in the year of the casualty: it waits for the year the
recoverable amount is ascertained.** 🛑 **So a basis-bearing `#7107` would most likely have been a 2025 item
TOO, and for the same reason ① gives — on 31 December 2024 this company held a destroyed truck and an
unsettled claim.** ⇒ **The loss branch would have turned on THE CLAIM'S STATUS, not on the 12/17/2024 date
alone.** ⛔ **The lesson survives — a qualifier written against a hypothetical earned its place — but the
sentence above overstated it, and *"a 2024 loss date takes it onto 2024's return"* is not a rule to reuse.**
🔴 **CITED FROM KNOWLEDGE, NOT FROM A SOURCE: nothing on this return rests on it** *(the basis is zero)*,
**and before anything ever does it is read off the current-year authority on irs.gov, like every rule here
that changes a figure.**

#### ⓑ 🛑 AND §3BD ②-bis ASKED A CLOSED QUESTION WHOSE ANSWER WAS IN NEITHER BRANCH

**It framed the date as a dichotomy:**

> ***"Either the 9-April credit is the settlement and §3C's JANUARY date is the right one, or the credit is
> not the settlement and §3BD ②'s identification is wrong."***

⛔ **BOTH BRANCHES ARE FALSE.** ✅ **The identification of the 9 April credit was RIGHT and the January date
was WRONG.** 🔑 **The two were never linked, and the reason nobody saw it is that all three candidate dates
the file held — `2025-01-01`, `2025-06-01`, `04/09/2025` — were inside 2025.** ⇒ **The paper reasoned
carefully WITHIN a candidate set that did not contain the answer.**

⚠️ **AND THE ELIMINATION ARGUMENT ITSELF WAS NEVER WRONG.** *"A settlement cannot arrive two months before
the truck was destroyed"* **is sound, and a 17 December 2024 loss settling on 9 April 2025 obeys it
perfectly.** 🔑 **What it could not do — and was used to do anyway — is ELECT A WINNER from a list of two
when the answer was a third thing nobody had proposed.**
☑️ **[`method.md`](../../pre-return-review/method.md) rule 1b is the closest existing rule — *a negative
belongs to the search that produced it* — and this is its sibling: a WINNER belongs to the candidate set that
produced it. Neither is a statement about the world.**

#### ②ⓑ 🧮 WHY THE 34,000 IS NOT ON THE RETURN — the arithmetic, in one place

🔑 **THE RULE, IN PLAIN WORDS: money you get back for a cost you never deducted is not income. You only pay
tax on the part that exceeds that cost.** *(The tax-benefit rule — §111.)*

```
  Insurance received, 9 April 2025                                    57,500.00
  less: the towing bill it reimbursed — a real cost the company
        bore and NEVER DEDUCTED, so getting it back is not income    (34,000.00)
                                                                     -----------
  Recovery attributable to the TRUCK                                  23,500.00
  less: the truck's ADJUSTED BASIS                                          0.00
        (50,000 of §179 + 28,145 of bonus consumed the whole
         78,145 of cost in 2021 — §3BL)
                                                                     -----------
  GAIN = §1245 ORDINARY INCOME, 2025                                  23,500.00
```

✅ **SO THE 34,000 APPEARS NOWHERE ON THE RETURN — NOT AS INCOME AND NOT AS A DEDUCTION.** **Both sides stay

never-deducted cost.**

### ④ 🚚 A VEHICLE DESTROYED IN 2024, SOLD OUT IN 2025 — the procedure, and why the opening balance sheet is untouchable

> 🗣️ **Lilian:** *"¿Cómo hacemos con este vehículo en la declaración de 2025? ¿Cómo lo sacamos de la
> declaración si se perdió en 2024? ¿Qué hacer en estos casos?"*

#### ④ⓐ 🔑 THE SHORT ANSWER: exactly as if it had been destroyed in 2025 — because the GAIN is a 2025 event

**A casualty gain is realized when the property is turned INTO MONEY, not when it is destroyed.** **The
truck was destroyed on 17 December 2024; the insurance arrived on 9 April 2025; the gain is 2025's.**
🔑 **This firm wrote that rule down months before it had the fact to apply it to** — **decision 13a ③:**
*"gain is realized when the PROCEEDS ARE RECEIVED, which may fall in a different tax year from the loss."*

#### ④ⓑ ☑️ THE FIVE STEPS, IN ORDER

| # | What | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | ⛔ **LEAVE THE 1/1/2025 SCHEDULE L ALONE.** **The opening column carries the truck at 78,145 on line 10a and 78,145 on line 10b** | **The opening column REPRODUCES THE FILED 2024 RETURN. It is not a statement of what was true on 1 January — it is a statement of what the prior return reported.** 🛑 **Changing it creates an unexplained break between the 2024 closing and the 2025 opening, which is wrong and is an audit flag** |
| **2** | ☑️ **DISPOSE of it in the 2025 depreciation schedule.** **`Date sold` = `04/09/2025` · proceeds `23,500` · adjusted basis `0`** | 🔑 **The date field takes the date the gain was REALIZED — when the money arrived — because that is what puts the event in 2025.** ⚠️ **The date of the LOSS is 12/17/2024 and it is recorded in this paper, not on the return** |
| **3** | ⛔ **DO NOT DELETE THE ASSET ROW** | **A disposal keeps the asset's history; a deletion destroys it, and ATX needs the history to compute recapture** |
| **4** | 🔑 **THE DISPOSAL GOES TO K-1 BOX 17 CODE K, NOT to Form 4797 and NOT to Form 4684** | **50,000 of its cost was expensed under §179 in 2021, and a §179 asset's disposal is reported to the SHAREHOLDER from the `179 Dispo` tab. ATX says so on the screen as you enter it: *"This disposition will NOT be reported on the 4797 per the form instructions"*** *(decision 87)* |
| **5** | ✅ **CLOSING Schedule L 10a and 10b each fall by 78,145** | **NET assets unchanged — the asset was fully depreciated, so cost and accumulated depreciation come off together** |

#### ④ⓒ ❓ "SHOULD 2024 BE AMENDED?" — NO, and here is the test

⚠️ **The 1/1/2025 balance sheet carries a truck that had already been destroyed. That looks wrong and a
reviewer will ask about it.** ✅ **It is harmless, and the reason is arithmetic:**

```
  2024 Schedule L line 10a  (cost)                     included  78,145
  2024 Schedule L line 10b  (accumulated depreciation) included (78,145)
                                                                --------
  Effect on 2024 NET assets                                          0
  Effect on 2024 income                                              0   (no depreciation left to take)
  Effect on 2024 depreciation                                        0   (fully written off in 2021)
```

☑️ **NOTHING ON THE 2024 RETURN WOULD CHANGE. No amendment is indicated.** 🔑 **The general test: an asset
whose cost and accumulated depreciation are equal is invisible to every number on the return, so leaving it
one year too long is a presentation point and not an error worth an amendment.**
⚠️ **IT WOULD BE DIFFERENT IF THE TRUCK HAD CARRIED BASIS** — **then 2024 would have been a casualty LOSS
year and the analysis would have had to decide WHEN the loss was sustained. Note that even then the answer
would probably still be 2025: a casualty loss covered by a claim still outstanding, with a reasonable
prospect of recovery, waits for the year the claim resolves.** 🔴 **CITED FROM KNOWLEDGE — nothing here rests
on it, and it is read off the current-year source before anything ever does.**

#### ⑤ⓐ 🔑 WHAT PREMIUM FINANCE IS — three parties, and the mechanism is the whole answer

**A commercial trucking policy is billed as ONE large annual premium, payable at inception. Most carriers do
not offer monthly billing. So a finance company steps in:**

```
   ZAKOM  ──── down payment 6,336.90 ────────────────────►  ASSUREDPARTNERS (the agency)
                                                                    │
   IPFS   ──── the rest of the premium, 29,256.10 ─────────────────►─┘  ──►  GREAT LAKES (the carrier)
     ▲                                                                       the policy is PAID IN FULL,
     │                                                                       at inception, in September 2025
     └──── ZAKOM repays IPFS, 3,138.90 a month ────────────────────
```

🛑 **THE ONE SENTENCE THAT ANSWERS HER QUESTION: THE INSURER IS PAID IN FULL, IN SEPTEMBER 2025, BY THE
COMPANY AND BY IPFS TOGETHER.** ⇒ **From that moment the company does not owe a PREMIUM. It owes a LOAN.**
🔑 **And repaying a loan is never an expense** — **only the INTEREST on it is.**

⚠️ **IPFS's security is not a guarantee, it is a power of attorney to CANCEL the policy** *(that is what a
premium finance agreement grants)*. **That matters here only because it is what makes IPFS a genuine
third-party lender rather than the seller extending credit — see ⓔ.**

#### ⑤ⓑ 📄 WHAT THE DOCUMENT ACTUALLY SAYS — and, just as important, what it does not

📄 **`IPFS Zakom Inc Proposal - Signed.pdf`** — **17 pages, an AssuredPartners insurance proposal signed by
the client on 09/18/2025** *(read 2026-09-30 through [`tools/redact-doc/`](../../../tools/redact-doc/); pages
13–16 carry no extractable text and are the signature pages)*.

| ✅ **PHYSICAL DAMAGE** | **Great Lakes.** **Comprehensive & Collision on `609,000` of trucks, `0` of trailers; `2,500` deductible under 100,000 of value and `5,000` over; rate `5.25%`; and a `Towing/Storage Ext - Accident` extension of `15,000`** |
| **APD subtotal** | **32,886** |

**STEP 1 — the amount IPFS actually lent.**
```

                                                  -----------
 = AMOUNT FINANCED  (the loan principal)           29,256.10
```

⚠️ **The down payment is `6,336.90 / 35,593.00 = 17.80%` of the premium — the standard structure for premium
finance, which is what makes the payment count below derivable at all.**

**STEP 2 — how many monthly payments? The document does not say, so it is DERIVED and the derivation is
shown.**
```

```
| n | Total of payments | Finance charge | Implied APR | Verdict |

| **9** | 28,250.10 | 🔴 **(1,006.00)** | — | ⛔ **IMPOSSIBLE — a negative finance charge** |

| **11** | 34,527.90 | 5,271.80 | **34.42%** | ⛔ **Rejected — no premium finance company charges 34%** |

everywhere it is used.**

**STEP 3 — the monthly rate. It is the `r` that makes ten payments of 3,138.90 worth 29,256.10 today:**
```
                     1 − (1 + r)^−n
      PV  =  PMT  ×  ──────────────           solve for r with PV = 29,256.10,
                            r                  PMT = 3,138.90, n = 10

      r  =  0.013003 per month   ⇒   nominal APR  =  r × 12  =  15.60%
```

#### ⑤ⓓ ⚖️ THE QUESTION SHE ASKED: the WHOLE premium, or only what was paid to IPFS?

🔑 **Two models, and they are not close.**

| | **MODEL A — deduct the PREMIUM** | **MODEL B — deduct the CASH** |
|---|---|---|
| **The idea** | **The insurer was paid in full in 2025; what remains is a loan** | **A cash-basis taxpayer deducts what left the bank** |
| **2025 insurance deduction** | **35,593.00** | **15,753.60** *(down payment 6,336.90 + 3 × 3,138.90)* |
| **2025 interest deduction** | **1,033.21** *(page 1 line 13)* | ⛔ **none — the interest is inside the instalments already deducted** |
| **Total 2025 deduction** | **36,626.21** | **15,753.60** |
| **Schedule L liability at 12/31** | **20,872.61** | ⛔ **none** |
| 🔴 **The difference in DEDUCTION** | **20,872.61** | |

🛑 **CORRECTION TO THIS PAPER, AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE THE FIGURE HAS BEEN QUOTED ALL WEEK.** §3BX ③ and
every surface citing it put the gap at **≈26,166** and called the liability by the same number. **Both are
wrong, for two separate reasons:**

1. ⛔ **Model B's deduction is NOT 9,426.70.** **That figure is only the cash paid to IPFS. The DOWN PAYMENT
   of 6,336.90 is also cash paid for insurance in 2025 and belongs in any cash model.** ⇒ **Model B is
   15,753.60.**
2. ⛔ **The LIABILITY is not the unpaid PREMIUM.** **The premium is fully paid. What is owed is loan
   PRINCIPAL, and three instalments have already repaid 8,383.49 of it.** ⇒ **20,872.61, not 26,166.**

```
   35,593.00  premium
  − 6,336.90  down payment  (paid by the company)
  − 8,383.49  principal repaid in the three 2025 instalments
  -----------
   20,872.61  owed to IPFS at 12/31/2025          ✅ ties to the amortization table
```

#### ⑤ⓔ ✅ WHY MODEL A IS RIGHT — the two gates it has to pass, and it passes both

🔑 **A cash-basis deduction has to clear TWO separate tests, and they are usually confused with each other.**

**GATE 1 — WAS IT *PAID* IN 2025?** ✅ **YES.**
**The general rule is that an expense paid with funds borrowed from a THIRD PARTY is paid when the third
party pays the provider** — **the borrowing and the payment are two separate events, and the later
repayments are repayments of a LOAN, not the expense.** **The IRS's own published analogue is the
credit-card rule: a charge on a third-party bank card is payment at the moment of the charge, because the
bank pays the provider; what the cardholder pays the bank later is debt service.**
⛔ **THE EXCEPTION, AND IT DOES NOT APPLY HERE: credit extended by the PROVIDER ITSELF is not payment — a
promise to pay the seller is just a promise.** 🔑 **IPFS is neither the carrier (Great Lakes) nor the agency
(AssuredPartners). It is a separate finance company, and the document says so on its face:
`Financing provided by IPFS`.**
🔴 **CITED FROM KNOWLEDGE. IRS Pub. 538's cash-method section does NOT address borrowed funds** *(checked on
irs.gov, 2026-09-30)*, **so this gate rests on general authority rather than on a current-year IRS page.**
⚖️ **IT IS JULIA'S TO CONFIRM — she is the EA who signs.**

**GATE 2 — IS IT A PREPAID EXPENSE THAT MUST BE SPREAD?** ✅ **NO — the 12-month rule covers it.**
**IRS Pub. 538, *Accounting Periods and Methods*, under `Expense paid in advance`, read on irs.gov
2026-09-30, verbatim:**

> ⚠️ ***"An expense you pay in advance is deductible only in the year to which it applies, unless the expense
> qualifies for the 12-month rule."***
>
> ✅ ***"Under the 12-month rule, a taxpayer is not required to capitalize amounts paid to create certain
> rights or benefits for the taxpayer that do not extend beyond the earlier of the following: 12 months after
> the right or benefit begins, or the end of the tax year after the tax year in which payment is made."***

| The test | This policy |
|---|---|
| **Not beyond 12 months after the benefit begins** | ✅ **A 12-month policy incepting September 2025 ends September 2026 — exactly 12 months, not beyond** |
| **Not beyond the end of the tax year AFTER the year of payment** | ✅ **Payment 2025 ⇒ the limit is 12/31/2026. The policy ends ~September 2026, comfortably inside** |

⛔ **ONE THING TO CONFIRM, AND THE DOCUMENT DOES NOT CARRY IT: the POLICY PERIOD.** **The proposal states no
effective or expiry date.** ✅ **The conclusion holds for ANY 12-month policy incepting in 2025**, ⚠️ **and
would fail only if the policy runs longer than twelve months, which a commercial auto physical damage policy
does not.** ☑️ **The declarations page settles it in one line; ask for it with the IPFS statement.**

balance by the whole amount.** **The liability, the interest and the equity plug are ONE entry, made in three
places.**

| ⇒ **REQUIRED closing equity** | **(162,063)** | **(182,936)** | 🔻 **−20,873** |


🔑 **AND THE 19,840 IS NOT A PLUG — IT IS A REAL NUMBER WITH A NAME:**
```
   20,872.61   the loan still owed
 −  1,033.21   the interest already deducted inside it
   ----------
   19,839.40   = 29,256.10 lent by IPFS − 9,416.70 repaid in 2025
```
✅ **It is the part of the premium the company DEDUCTED but has not yet PAID.** **On a set of books with no
equity section, where everything unexplained becomes distributions** *(decision 104)*, **that is exactly
where it lands.**

⚠️ **AND THIS IS WHY §3BS's open-items rows 2 and 3 say the two halves *"largely cancel"* — they do, on
TAXABLE INCOME. They do NOT cancel on the BALANCE SHEET.** 🔑 **THAT IS MEASURED AGAINST THE DRAFT, WHICH
ALREADY CARRIES MODEL A's 35,593 OF INSURANCE.** **From the draft, recording IPFS moves taxable income by
only the `1,033.21` of interest — while it takes the required equity DOWN `20,873`, of which `19,839.40`
lands in the residual.** 🛑 **So "it nets out" is true of the tax and false of the K-1.**

⛔ 🆕 **AND BETWEEN THE TWO MODELS IT IS THE OTHER WAY ROUND — AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS PARAGRAPH HAD IT
INVERTED, AND THE REVIEW CAUGHT IT.** **The baselines are different and the relationship reverses:**

| | Draft → Model A *(recording IPFS)* | Model A vs Model B *(if Julia rules against gate 1)* |
|---|---|---|
| **Taxable income** | 🔻 **1,033.21 only** — *the interest* | 🔴 **20,872.61 apart** — **Model A deducts 36,626.21, Model B 15,753.60** |
| **Required closing equity** | 🔻 **20,873 lower** — *the new liability* | 🔴 **20,873 apart** — **(182,936) against (162,063): Model B carries NO liability** |
| **Reported distributions / K-1 16d** | 🔺 **+19,839.40**, to 132,583 | ✅ **THE SAME — 132,583 against 132,582.40, to sixty cents** |

🔑 **THE STRUCTURE, because it is not a coincidence: Model A's extra liability (20,872.61) and its extra
deduction (20,872.61) are the SAME number, so they cancel in the plug.** **Under Model B the loss becomes a
profit — book income is 19,839.40 higher, M-2 line 6 runs to 30,688.40 and line 7 takes all of it — and
required equity stays at (162,063). The residual is untouched.**
⇒ ⛔ **SO IF JULIA RULES AGAINST GATE 1, THE K-1 DOES NOT MOVE. The tax does, by 20,872.61.** **A session
keying Model B off the old sentence would have expected the opposite of both.**

### ② 🧮 HOW THE INTEREST RATE WAS DERIVED — step by step, because she asked for exactly this

> 🗣️ *"Quiero también que quede bien explicado cómo llegamos a esta tasa de interés, cómo se hizo ese
> cálculo de la tasa de interés."*

⛔ **THE RATE IS NOWHERE ON ANY DOCUMENT THE FIRM HOLDS.** **The proposal prints a premium, a down payment
and a monthly payment. It does not print an APR, a finance charge, a payment count or a due date.** 🔑 **So
the rate is SOLVED FOR, and here is every step.**

#### ②ⓐ THE THREE INPUTS, AND WHERE EACH ONE COMES FROM

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **The premium** | **35,593.00** | 📄 **The signed proposal's printed `Total`** *(and the client's own arithmetic uses it: 79,963 − 35,593 = 44,370)* |
| **The down payment** | **6,336.90** | 📄 **The proposal — ✅ and now the BANK, 09/19/2025** |
| **The monthly payment** | **3,138.90** | 📄 **The proposal — ✅ and now the BANK, three times** |

#### ②ⓑ STEP 1 — what IPFS actually lent

```
      amount financed  =  premium  −  down payment
                       =  35,593.00  −  6,336.90
                       =  29,256.10
```
⚠️ **And the down payment is `6,336.90 / 35,593.00 = 17.80%` of the premium — which is the standard shape of
a premium-finance plan and is what makes step 2 possible at all.**

#### ②ⓒ STEP 2 — how many payments? The document is silent, so it is BOUNDED and then chosen

**If the instalments carried NO interest at all, the number of payments would be:**
```
      29,256.10 ÷ 3,138.90  =  9.3204
```
🔑 **So there must be AT LEAST TEN — nine payments could not even repay the principal.** **Then each
candidate is tested by the finance charge and the rate it implies:**

| n | Total of payments `n × 3,138.90` | Finance charge `total − 29,256.10` | Implied nominal APR | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **9** | **28,250.10** | 🔴 **(1,006.00)** | — | ⛔ **IMPOSSIBLE. A lender cannot charge a negative fee** |
| ✅ **10** | **31,389.00** | **2,132.90** | **15.60%** | ✅ **ACCEPTED. An ordinary premium-finance rate, and 17.8% down + 10 payments is the standard plan** |
| **11** | **34,527.90** | **5,271.80** | **34.42%** | ⛔ **REJECTED. No licensed premium finance company charges 34%** |
| **12** | **37,666.80** | **8,410.70** | **49.43%** | ⛔ **REJECTED, and it gets worse from here** ⓘ *(this row read 50.3%; solving the annuity gives 49.43%)* |

⇒ ☑️ **TEN. It is the ONLY count that produces a finance charge a real lender would write.**

#### ②ⓓ STEP 3 — solving for the rate

**With the count fixed, the monthly rate is whatever makes ten payments of 3,138.90 worth 29,256.10 today.
That is the ordinary present-value-of-an-annuity equation, solved for `r`:**

```
                        1 − (1 + r)^−n
      PV   =   PMT  ×  ────────────────
                              r

      29,256.10  =  3,138.90  ×  [ 1 − (1 + r)^−10 ] ÷ r
```

⛔ **There is no algebraic solution for `r` — it is found numerically, by bisection: try a rate, compute the
present value, and narrow.** ✅ **The answer:**

```
      r  =  0.013003  per month
      nominal APR  =  r × 12  =  15.60%
```

☑️ **AND THE CHECK THAT MAKES IT TRUSTWORTHY — run it backwards.** **Amortize at 0.013003 and the balance
must reach exactly zero on the tenth payment. It does** *(§3CE ⑤ⓒ STEP 4)*, **and the total interest over
the ten payments comes to 2,132.90 — the same finance charge the count implied. The two derivations agree,
which they only do if the rate is right.**

#### ②ⓔ ⚠️ WHAT THE ESTIMATE IS SENSITIVE TO — stated honestly

| If this is wrong | 2025 interest | 12/31/2025 balance |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ **Nothing is — the working case** | **1,033.21** | **20,872.61** |
| **The premium is 35,293** *(the proposal's own parts add to 300 less than its printed Total)* | 1,176.23 | 20,715.63 |
| **Eleven payments** *(rejected at 34% APR)* | 2,317.66 | 22,157.06 |
| 🔑 **THE SPREAD** | **1,033 – 2,318** | 🔑 **20,716 – 22,157** |

✅ **THE LIABILITY IS THE ROBUST ONE — every branch lands within 1,441 of 20,873, and it is the figure that
moves the balance sheet.** ⚠️ **The interest is softer and it is the smaller number; the whole of it is
1,033.21 against a page-1 line 13 of 57,563.64, so a 100% error in it moves line 13 by under 2%.**

### ③ 📝 THE NOTE FOR JULIA ON IPFS — written to be read on its own

> 🗣️ *"vamos a hacer una nota para Julia explicando toda la situación con IPFS."*

🔑 **This is the note. It assumes she has read nothing else.**

> **THE SITUATION.** The company's truck physical-damage policy for 2025 is billed as one annual premium of
> **35,593**, payable when the policy starts. The carrier does not bill it monthly, so the client financed it
> through **IPFS**, a premium finance company: he paid a down payment of **6,336.90** and IPFS paid the rest
> of the premium — **29,256.10** — to the carrier at inception, in September 2025. He repays IPFS **3,138.90**
> a month.
>
> **WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE RETURN.** From the day the policy started the company does not owe a PREMIUM —
> the insurer is paid. It owes a **LOAN**. So the 2025 insurance deduction is the whole **35,593** (already
> inside the client's `Insurance` caption of 79,963); the instalments are debt service; only the **interest**
> inside them is deductible; and the **unpaid loan balance at 31 December 2025 is a liability on Schedule L**.
>
> **WHAT WE HOLD.** A signed AssuredPartners proposal, and nothing else. It states the premium, the down
> payment and the monthly payment. It does **not** state the number of payments, the finance charge, the
> interest rate, the payment dates or the policy period. **The client has told us he cannot obtain a
> year-end statement from IPFS and that there is no further document.** So those figures are **estimated**.
>
> **WHAT THE BANK PROVES.** The September–December 2025 statements were read line by line. They show the
> **6,336.90 down payment as an outgoing wire on 19 September**, the day after he signed; an IPFS
> **account-verification debit of 10.00 on 23 September**; and **three instalments of exactly 3,138.90**, on
> 21 October, 20 November and 22 December. **Total cash out in 2025: 15,763.60.** So the plan on the proposal
> is the plan that ran.
>
> **WHAT IS ESTIMATED, AND HOW.** The number of payments is **ten**. It cannot be fewer — nine payments of
> 3,138.90 do not repay 29,256.10 — and eleven would imply a 34% interest rate, which no premium finance
> company charges. Ten implies a finance charge of **2,132.90** and a rate of **15.60% a year**, which is
> ordinary. Amortizing at that rate, the three 2025 instalments carry **1,033.21 of interest** and
> **8,383.49 of principal**, leaving **20,872.61** owed at 31 December 2025.
>
> **THE THREE FIGURES ON THE RETURN.**
> • Page 1 line 20 — **nothing to add**; the 35,593 is already in the client's Insurance caption.
> • Page 1 line 13 `Interest` — **add 1,033.21** *(estimated)*.
> • Schedule L **line 17**, `Mortgages, notes, bonds payable in less than 1 year` — **20,872.61**
> *(estimated)*. It is line 17 and not line 20 because the plan clears in July 2026.
>
> **AND THEY DO NOT STAND ALONE.** Recording the liability moves the equity section: Schedule L line 23 goes
> to **(193,752)**, M-2 lines 6 and 7 to **9,816** with line 8 still zero, and reported distributions to
> **132,583**. The sheet then balances at **(182,936)**.
>
> **WHAT NEEDS YOUR RULING.** One step of the analysis does not rest on a current-year IRS page: that an
> expense paid with money borrowed from a **third party** is *paid* when that third party pays the provider.
> The other half — that a 12-month policy is not a prepaid to be spread — is quoted verbatim from IRS
> Publication 538 and is not in doubt.
>
> **HOW EXPOSED IS THE ESTIMATE.** If the payment count were eleven instead of ten, the liability would be
> 22,157 instead of 20,873 and the interest 2,318 instead of 1,033. Every branch we can construct puts the
> liability within about 1,400 of the figure used. The interest is the softer number and the smaller one:
> the whole of it is 1,033.21 against a line 13 of 57,563.64.

#### ④ⓑ ☑️ AND THE DATES MOVE NO FIGURE — here is the test, not the assertion

⚠️ **The half-year convention gives every asset half a year's depreciation whatever month it went in — UNLESS
the MID-QUARTER convention is triggered, and that is a real test with a real threshold.** ✅ **It is not
triggered here, and the arithmetic is this:**

```
   Q1  1837 63,195 + 1839 105,550 + Reitnouer 70,540   =  239,285
   Q2  none                                            =        0
   Q3  1840 115,550 + Benson 43,650                    =  159,200
   Q4  146 23,000                                      =   23,000
                                                         ---------
                                          TOTAL           421,485

   Q4 share  =  23,000 / 421,485  =  5.46%      threshold 40%      ⇒ NOT triggered
```

✅ **So HALF-YEAR applies to all six, and a date that is off by a month or two changes nothing.** 🔑 **That is
why the undocumented dates on rows 1, 3 and 6 are not a blocker** — ⚠️ **and it is worth re-running this test
if any 2025 addition is ever added, moved into Q4, or removed.**

### ⑤ 💸 THE FREIGHT CHARGES AND THE LIABILITY/CARGO PREMIUMS — the question stated properly, and what the bank says

> 🗣️ **Lilian:** *"añade una nota que explique las deducciones de los freight charges que fueron pagados al
> cliente para pagar parte de la liability and cargo coverage… no sabemos si en ese income que nos dio el
> cliente ya está reducido ese pago del seguro o si no lo está. Porque, si en ese income ya se dedujo el
> seguro, entonces… no se puede deducir en la cuenta de insurance nuevamente porque ya se declaró menos
> income… Quiero también que me diga si hay alguna forma de que sepamos eso mirando los statements del
> banco."*

#### ⑤ⓐ 🔑 WHAT THE CLIENT TOLD US, AND WHY IT OPENS A QUESTION

🗣️ **Oleg, 2026-09-30:** *"$35,593 is Physical Damage coverage only. Liability and cargo coverage was done
through partner's insurance policy. Partner had deducted these premiums on weekly base accordingly from
freight charges paid to me. Therefore, remaining $44.4 (from 79.9K) are Lia/Cargo insurance premiums."*

✅ **HIS ARITHMETIC IS EXACT: `79,963 − 35,593 = 44,370`.** **So his `Insurance` caption is 35,593 of truck
physical damage plus 44,370 of liability and cargo.**

🛑 **AND THE 44,370 NEVER LEFT HIS BANK.** **His freight partner kept it out of what it paid him, week by
week. He never wrote a cheque for it.** ⇒ **Which raises the one question this section exists for.**

#### ⑤ⓑ 🧮 THE QUESTION, AS ARITHMETIC — because in words it keeps slipping

**Suppose in one week the freight earned is 100 and the partner keeps 10 of insurance, paying him 90.**

| | **What he booked as revenue** | **What he booked as insurance** | **Profit** | **Correct?** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ✅ **GROSS** | **100** *(what he BILLED)* | **10** | **90** | ✅ **RIGHT** |
| 🔴 **NET** | **90** *(what he RECEIVED)* | **10** | **80** | ⛔ **WRONG — the 10 is deducted TWICE**, once by never being counted as income and once as an expense |

🔑 **THAT IS EXACTLY LILIAN'S POINT, and it is worth having in one line: *if the income figure is already net
of the insurance, the insurance cannot be deducted again, because the deduction has already been taken by
reporting less income*.**

⚠️ **AND THE EXPOSURE RUNS AGAINST THE CLIENT EITHER WAY IT IS RESOLVED:** **on the NET reading his gross
receipts AND his net income are each understated by ≈44,370.** ⛔ **This is not a question whose comfortable
answer is "leave it" — it is a question whose comfortable answer is that he reported GROSS.**

#### ⑤ⓒ 🏦 CAN THE BANK ANSWER IT? — YES, PARTLY, AND IT POINTS AT *GROSS*

> 🗣️ *"¿hay alguna forma de que sepamos eso mirando los statements del banco: cuánto dinero entró a la
> compañía durante el año?"*

✅ **THE LOGIC IS SOUND AND THE DATA EXISTS.** **If his revenue figure is the CASH THAT REACHED HIM, then his
deposits ought to equal it. If it is the freight he BILLED, his deposits ought to be LOWER — by the
withheld insurance, and by anything billed in December and collected in January.**

**All twelve 2025 statements were parsed in full and their sums equal the statements' own printed totals**
*(§3E ⑤)*:

```
   TOTAL MONEY IN, 2025, all 168 credits                      1,337,154.15

   less the credits that are NOT freight revenue:
        the insurance settlement, 9 April                       (57,500.00)
        the Audi, a plain DEPOSIT on 21 August                  (19,500.00)
        the Porsche proceeds wired in, August                   (18,000.00)
        Robinhood Securities, 27 October                        (13,035.00)
        OWL LAND, "For Truck 1834 and Trailer 1011", 26 June    (10,000.00)
        the ZAKOM 7807 offsets coming back in                    (3,727.20)
                                                              -------------
   FREIGHT-LIKE DEPOSITS                                       1,215,391.95

   REPORTED Sales Revenue                                      1,289,315.00
   ⇒ reported revenue EXCEEDS banked receipts by                   73,923.05
```

| The reading | What the cash SHOULD have been | Banked | Left unexplained |
|---|---|---|---|
| ✅ **GROSS — he billed 1,289,315 and the partner withheld 44,370** | **1,244,945.00** | **1,215,391.95** | **29,553.05** — 🔑 **an ordinary year-end receivable: freight hauled in December and paid in January** |
| 🔴 **NET — he reported the cash that reached him** | **1,289,315.00** | **1,215,391.95** | **73,923.05** — ⛔ **which would have to be money received OUTSIDE this account, and decision 11 rules this is the company's ONLY account** |

⇒ ⚠️ 🆕 **NARROWED IN REVIEW — THE BANK EXCLUDES ONE READING, IT DOES NOT SETTLE THE QUESTION.**
⛔ **AN EARLIER VERSION SAID *"THE BANK POINTS AT GROSS… under the net reading the remainder has no name"*.
THAT WAS TOO WIDE, AND THE REVIEW WAS RIGHT: 73,923 has exactly the same name — a year-end receivable —
it is simply a bigger one.** 🔑 **WHAT THE COMPARISON REALLY DOES:**

| The reading | Is it excluded? |
|---|---|
| ⛔ **His figure is the CASH ACTUALLY BANKED** | ✅ **EXCLUDED.** **He banked 1,215,392 and reported 1,289,315 — a cash figure cannot exceed the cash** |
| ⚠️ **His figure is BILLED, GROSS of the withheld premiums** | ⛔ **NOT excluded — remainder 29,553, about eight days of freight** |
| ⚠️ **His figure is BILLED, NET of them** *(what the weekly settlements said was due him)* | ⛔ **NOT excluded — remainder 73,923, about twenty days of freight** |

🛑 **AND THE TWO THAT SURVIVE ARE ON OPPOSITE SIDES OF THE QUESTION: the first is fine, the second
double-deducts the premiums.** ⇒ ⛔ **SO THE 44,370 IS NOT SETTLED BY THE BANK.** **What the bank does is
retire the crudest reading and narrow the ask.**

⛔ **AND IT IS CORROBORATION, NOT PROOF — every limitation, named** *(rule 1b)*:

1. ⚠️ **The non-revenue subtractions are IDENTIFICATIONS, not captions.** **The Audi 19,500 is a bare
   `DEPOSIT`; the Robinhood 13,035 is unexplained; `HUNTINGTON BP MERCH PMT` 15,000 + 13,216 is left IN as
   revenue on its caption alone.**
2. 🔴 **`USA FLORIDA FREIGHT` — 434,132.39 across 35 deposits — is left IN as revenue, and the client's own
   asset sheet calls that relationship a *loan*.** **If it were a loan, freight receipts would be ~781,000
   against a reported 1,289,315, which no reading survives.** ⇒ 🔑 **So this comparison is itself evidence
   that USA Florida Freight is a CUSTOMER — worth noting, because §3E ⑤ left that open.**
3. ⚠️ **A cash-basis taxpayer's own spreadsheet may still carry a BILLED figure.** **The comparison tests
   what his number IS, not what it ought to be.**
4. ⚠️ **The 29,553 is not independently verified as a receivable.** **It is the size of one that would be
   ordinary on a 1.2M book — about eight days of freight.**
5. 🔴 **THE 57,500 IS THE SUBTRACTION THAT COULD REVERSE THE WHOLE COMPARISON, and it rests on an
   identification this paper calls UNESTABLISHED.** **The bank prints it `OWL LAND OF ILLI ACH Pmt` — the
   company's own freight CUSTOMER, on the same instrument as every other OWL LAND freight payment — and
   §3BD ④ says in terms that the two readings are not settled.** ⛔ **Add it back and freight-like deposits
   become 1,272,892, which moves both remainders by 57,500 and changes the shape of the answer.**
6. ⚠️ **The 19,500 and the 18,000 are subtracted on the same basis** — **a bare `DEPOSIT` matched to the
   client's asset sheet by amount, and a wire matched to his note about the Porsche. Neither carries a
   caption that says what it is.**
7. ⚠️ **AND THE COMPARISON ASSUMES HIS 1,289,315 EXCLUDES ALL SEVEN OF THOSE ITEMS.** **Nobody has tested
   that against his spreadsheet. If any of them is inside his revenue line, the subtraction removes it

✅ **NOTHING SEPARATE. IT IS ALREADY TAXED, INSIDE THE 23,500.**

```
   Insurance received                                57,500.00
   less the towing it reimbursed — never deducted   (34,000.00)
                                                    -----------
   Recovery for the TRUCK                            23,500.00
   less the truck's adjusted basis                         0.00
                                                    -----------
   §1245 ORDINARY INCOME, 2025                       23,500.00
```

🔑 **His own split was `20,000 + 34,000 = 54,000` against `57,500` received.** ⛔ **The 3,500 is not
"unallocated" and it is not a loose end: it is simply MORE recovery than his estimate of the two parts, and
every dollar of recovery above the never-deducted 34,000 is gain against a zero basis.** ⇒ ✅ **It is inside
the 23,500 that goes to K-1 box 17 code K. There is no second entry and no second decision.**

⛔ **AND IT IS WHY THE CLIENT IS NOT ASKED TO SPLIT THE TWO CHEQUES** *(decision 115)*: **the answer is
23,500 whichever way they divide.** ⚠️ **The only thing that would change it is if the 34,000 of towing had
been DEDUCTED in 2024 — ⑧ below, and decision 133.**

### ⑦ 🔴 THE AUDI's 72,000 MILES — ⛔ **DO NOT KEY 72,000. IT IS AN ODOMETER READING, AND THE BOX ASKS FOR THE YEAR**

> 🗣️ **Lilian:** *"Voy a poner las 72,000 millas en el Audi que fue vendido. Voy a poner ese valor en ATX."*

🗣️ **THE SOURCE — Oleg, 2026-09-30:** *"72K miles on Audi at the time of trade in."*

🛑 **CAUGHT BY THE REVIEW, AND IT WOULD HAVE GONE ON THE FORM: an earlier version of this sub-section told
her to key `72,000` into Form 4562 Part V. THAT IS WRONG, and the paper already held what makes it wrong.**

| | |
|---|---|
| ⛔ **WHAT `72,000` ACTUALLY IS** | 🔑 **THE ODOMETER AT DISPOSAL — a lifetime total.** **The car went into service on 1 February 2021 and left on 21 August 2025, so 72,000 is four and a half years of driving, about 15,800 a year** |
| 🔴 **WHY IT CANNOT GO IN PART V** | 📄 **Form 4562 Part V Section B asks for miles driven DURING THE YEAR** — **line 30 `Total business/investment miles driven during the year`, line 31 commuting, line 32 other personal, line 33 `Total miles driven during the year`.** ⛔ **Every one of them is a for-the-year figure** *(read on irs.gov: the business-use percentage is business miles "during the year" ÷ total miles for all purposes)* |
| 🧮 **AND THE PAPER ALREADY HELD THE OTHER HALF** | 🗣️ **The client, by TaxDome message on 2025-08-20:** *"As of 12/31/24 Audi mileage was 65000miles."* *(§3BK ③)*. ⇒ 🔑 **`72,000 − 65,000 = 7,000` — THE 2025 MILES.** ✅ **§3BJ C5 wrote the subtraction months ago and said only the second half was missing. It arrived on 30 September, and this sub-section keyed the raw reading instead of doing the sum** |
| ⌨️ **SO WHAT IS KEYED** | **At the schedule's 100% business use: line 30 `7,000` · line 31 `0` · line 32 `0` · line 33 `7,000`** — **the same presentation the FILED 2024 return used, where the Audi carried `15,000 / 0 / 0`** |
| 🔴 **WHAT KEYING 72,000 WOULD HAVE DONE** | **The Audi is on the schedule at 100% business use, so `72,000` in that table asserts SEVENTY-TWO THOUSAND BUSINESS MILES for the 233 days of 2025 it was owned *(1 January to 21 August)* — nearly FIVE TIMES the prior year's whole-year figure — on the one asset whose business-use support is already missing** *(`Form 4562 Part V Section A` lines 24a and 24b are both unanswered — §3AX row 10)* **and which is §280F-capped** |
| ⚠️ **AND BOTH READINGS ARE THE CLIENT'S STATEMENTS, not documents** | **65,000 and 72,000 are both things he told us. Say so to Julia; there is no odometer disclosure and no bill of sale** |
| ⛔ **IT STILL DOES NOT CHANGE A FIGURE ON THE RETURN** | **The Audi is disposed of at 19,500 against a keyed cost of 50,020, and mileage does not enter that computation. What it changes is what the FORM SAYS** |
| 🔴 **NOR DOES IT MOVE DECISION 65** | **He calls it a *"trade in"* for the second time; the LEASE says `Net trade-in allowance N/A` and the BANK shows a plain 19,500 DEPOSIT on 21 August. It is a SALE** |
| ⚠️ **AND THE SEVEN OTHER ZERO-MILE ROWS ARE THE REAL ITEM** | **They are there because seven of the eight pre-2025 assets sit on a LISTED-PROPERTY category they should never have had** *(§3BR — a freight tractor is not listed property)*. **That is a category fix, not a mileage fix** |

### ⑧ 🚚 THE TRUCK WRECKED IN 2024 — confirming what she remembered, because she remembered it right

> 🗣️ **Lilian:** *"Creo que me habías dicho que vamos a tratar como si se hubiese hecho la disposición de
> este asset en la misma fecha que se recibió el dinero, ¿cierto?"*

✅ **CORRECT, AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHAT IS KEYED.** **`Date sold` = `04/09/2025`, the day the 57,500 arrived.**

🔑 **THE REASON, IN ONE SENTENCE: a casualty GAIN is realized when the property is turned INTO MONEY, not
when it is destroyed.** **The truck was destroyed on 17 December 2024; the money arrived on 9 April 2025; the
gain is 2025's.** **This firm wrote that rule down months before it had the fact to apply it to —
decision 13a ③.**

☑️ **THE FIVE STEPS, restated because she asked for them in one place:**

| # | | |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | ⛔ **Leave the 1/1/2025 Schedule L alone** | **The opening column reproduces the FILED 2024 return — it is not a statement of what was true on 1 January** |
| **2** | ☑️ **Dispose of it in the 2025 schedule** | **`Date sold` `04/09/2025` · proceeds `23,500` · adjusted basis `0`** |
| **3** | ⛔ **Do NOT delete the asset row** | **A disposal keeps the history; a deletion destroys it, and the software needs the history to compute recapture** |
| **4** | 🔑 **It goes to K-1 box 17 code K** | **NOT Form 4684 and NOT the corporation's Form 4797 — 50,000 of its cost was §179'd in 2021** *(decision 87)* |
| **5** | ✅ **Closing Schedule L 10a and 10b each fall by 78,145** | **Net assets unchanged — cost and accumulated depreciation come off together** |

✅ **AND NO 2024 AMENDMENT IS INDICATED.** **The asset's cost and its accumulated depreciation were EQUAL at
78,145, so on the 2024 return it was invisible to every number: not income, not net assets, not
depreciation.** 🔑 **The general test — an asset whose cost equals its accumulated depreciation can sit one
year too long on a balance sheet without changing anything on it.**

📝 **AND THE ONE THING STILL OPEN ON IT IS JULIA'S, NOT THE CLIENT'S:** **whether the 34,000 of towing was
DEDUCTED on the 2024 return.** ⚖️ **Lilian ruled 2026-09-30 that the return is prepared on the assumption
that it was not** *(decision 133)*. ⛔ **If Julia rules otherwise it is +34,000 on page 1 line 5 —
CORPORATE other income, with nothing to offset it — and every equity figure re-derives from there.**
